title: What is a black hole?
subtitle: Extreme Severity
subject: sciences
description: A black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner. It is a region where gravity is so strong that even light cannot escape.

hero.hook: Nothing comes out, not even light. However, we ended up photographing its shadow.

blocks.text: A black hole is a region of **space-time**, the fabric that unites space and time, where gravity is so intense that the speed needed to escape exceeds that of light. Nothing comes out: no matter, no light signal.

It is not a “hole” in the sense of a tunnel. It is an extreme concentration of material which bends this fabric very strongly. Long a pure theory resulting from Einstein's equations, black holes are today observed in several ways.

A stellar black hole is often born from the death of a very massive star, at least **20 to 25 times the mass of the Sun. During its life, the star holds on thanks to a balance: gravity pulls towards the center, the pressure of **nuclear**merger** pushes outwards. At the heart of the star, hydrogen transforms into helium.

blocks.caption: A black hole surrounded by its incandescent accretion disk.

blocks.text: When the fuel runs out, the pressure drops. The heart of the star is crushed. An explosion of **supernova** can then light up the galaxy. If the remaining core is massive enough, there is nothing to stop the compression.

At the center, the theory describes a : a point where density and curvature become extreme, and where our current equations stop working well. Around it, we find the : an invisible border. Once crossed, no return possible to the rest of the universe. [[The gravitational singularity]] [[Event horizon]]
If you fell towards a black hole, gravity would pull much harder on your feet than on your head. This stretching is called “spaghettification”.

Contrary to popular belief, a black hole does not suck in everything that passes in the distance. Its gravity depends on its mass and distance, as with any object. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would continue to orbit. But without light and heat, we would freeze.

There are also **supermassive black holes**, of millions to billions of solar masses, at the heart of almost all galaxies. In the Milky Way, it is **Sagittarius A***, about **4 million** solar masses.

They are often spotted thanks to the : a ring of gas and dust which rotates very quickly around them. Friction heats this material until it becomes extremely bright in X-rays or radio waves. We then see the shadow of the black hole on this luminous background. [[Accretion disk]]

In **April 2019**, the Event Horizon Telescope project releases the first image of a black hole. By combining eight radio telescopes using the , researchers are creating a virtual telescope the size of Earth. [[Interferometry]]

The target is **M87***, the supermassive black hole in the galaxy Messier 87, **55 million** light years away. We see a bright ring around a dark area: the silhouette of the event horizon. In **2022**, an image of our neighbor Sagittarius A* follows.
Since **2015**, the LIGO and Virgo observatories have also detected **gravitational waves**: small vibrations of space-time produced when two black holes merge.

In **1974**, the British physicist **Stephen Hawking** showed that a black hole would not be totally black. Due to quantum effects near the horizon, it would emit very weak radiation: . [[Hawking radiation]]

Result: an isolated black hole would slowly lose mass and eventually evaporate. For a stellar black hole, this would take times fantastically longer than the current age of the universe. This idea also raises the information paradox: what happens to the information of what fell inside if the black hole disappears?
Near a black hole, time also passes more slowly for a distant observer, a relativistic effect of **time dilation**. These objects remain among the best laboratories for testing the limits of physics.
A black hole is often formed by the collapse of a massive star. It is bounded by the event horizon, a boundary photographed for the first time in **2019** around M87*.
